title: Energy densities, bound water, store sizes and allocation, store time-courses and expenditure checks for a healthy adult (task 5563, LN-5 {R-STORES})
source: Abstracts, article pages and PDFs listed in sources.json under ST-* keys. Where a page returned a browser check, an HTTP error or a scan, the Note says relayed and names the search result the figure came from. A null Value, Low and High means no opened page gave the figure. Rows marked derived are my arithmetic. Task 5563, LN-5.
rows: Energy content per kg change of body fat
9.44 kcal/g (derived, 4.184 kJ/kcal). Stated for 'body fat' with no water; adipose tissue is a different quantity (Hall 2008 summary relayed: the 3,500 kcal rule assumes adipose of 87% fat).
Energy content per kg change of lean tissue
Adults; lean tissue with its intracellular water (protein plus 1.6 g water per g)
1.82 kcal/g (derived). Equals rho_P/(1+h_P) = 19.7/2.6 = 7.58 (derived), so it is a hydrated figure per kg of lean tissue, not per kg of protein.
Adults; Hall Lancet appendix and Chow and Hall 2008

4.21 kcal/g (derived). Hydrated at 2.7 g water per g it is 17.6/3.7 = 4.76 MJ/kg = 1.14 kcal/g (derived). The appendix does not say whether this is metabolisable or gross energy; the Chow and Hall text calls the three values 'energy densities'.
Adults; Chow and Hall 2008 constants rho_F 39.5, rho_G 17.6, rho_P 19.7

4.71 kcal/g (derived). Not the Atwater 4 kcal/g general factor; the page does not say how 19.7 was obtained (the cited source is not on the text read). The built library row uses 'protein 4 kcal/g' (nutrition.body_composition source line).
Intracellular water bound per g of body protein
Adults; 'reasonable estimate' of the hydration coefficient h_P

Fat is taken to hold no water (same page). 1.6/2.6 = 61.5% water by mass of the hydrated lean unit (derived), lower than the 0.73 of whole fat-free mass because that figure also includes extracellular water.
Water stored with each g of glycogen
Adults; Hall Lancet appendix (cites its ref 4) and Chow and Hall h_G
Compare the library row glycogen-bound-water, 3 g/g (King 2017, itself citing Maughan 2007).
Range only; abstract states '3 to 4 parts water per part glycogen' and 0.45 mmol potassium per g glycogen. Hydrated form.
Muscle glycogen 4 h after 150 min of cycling at 65% VO2max in heat, 250 g carbohydrate in 400 mL (REHLOW) or in full fluid replacement (REHFULL)

79 +/- 15 (REHLOW) and 87 +/- 18 (REHFULL), p = 0.20. Muscle water after recovery 3459 +/- 324 and 3814 +/- 222 g/kg dry muscle (p < 0.05). The abstract also prints a water-to-glycogen ratio of 1:3 (REHLOW) and 1:17 (REHFULL) whose definition I could not check, so no ratio is a Value.
Water fraction of fat-free body mass
Mammals, review of in vitro and in vivo evidence
Review abstract: 'stable at approximately 0.73 in mammals'. Includes extracellular water, so it cannot be added to a lean term that already holds 1.6 g water per g protein (the A9 non-overlap rule).
Body glycogen at baseline in the Hall Lancet model
Model input, not a measurement. The built library row says up to 400 g (nutrition.body_composition.glycogen).
Healthy men after glycogen depletion then 7 days of 86%-carbohydrate overfeeding (3,642 to 4,930 kcal/d)

Relayed from a search result quoting the abstract: capacity 'approximately 15 g/kg body weight', accommodating a gain of about 500 g before net lipid synthesis adds to fat mass. 15 g/kg x 70 kg = 1,050 g (derived) is not the 500 g gain; the abstract text I saw does not reconcile them, so a total cap is open.
Lipid synthesised per day from massive carbohydrate intake after glycogen was filled
Same overfeeding; about 475 g carbohydrate per day
Relayed from the same search result. RQ above 1.0 after about 3 days (relayed, Hellerstein 1999 citing this paper).
Glycogen stored in 24 h after a 500 g carbohydrate meal
Healthy volunteers after 3 to 6 days on high-carbohydrate (170 +/- 2 g), mixed (197 +/- 11) or high-fat (278 +/- 6) diets

34% to 56% of the 500 g (derived). Net lipid synthesised only 0.8 +/- 0.5, 3.4 +/- 0.6 and 9 +/- 1 g (high-fat, mixed, high-carbohydrate). Prior diet changes the answer, so a single fraction (built: 0.8 x carbohydrate to glycogen) is outside this range. +/- as printed, SD or SEM not stated.
Net lipid synthesised in 24 h after a 500 g carbohydrate meal
Oxidised plus converted to fat: 222 +/- 5 (high-fat), 300 +/- 13 (mixed), 331 +/- 7 g (high-carbohydrate). Postabsorptive nonprotein RQ correlated with net lipogenesis (r = 0.82).
Thermic effect of the 500 g carbohydrate load
A feeding cost the built expenditure path does not carry (it charges MET x RMR only). The abstract says the percentage rose with net lipogenesis (r = 0.71).
Liver glycogen concentration before a liquid mixed meal
Healthy adults, 13C NMR; fasting hours before the meal not on the abstract
+/- 22 as printed. Peak 316 +/- 19 mmol/L at about 318 min (row below).
Liver glycogen concentration at its post-meal peak
Same; peak about 318 min after the meal

+/- 19 as printed. Falls after the peak at 0.26 mmol/L/min (15.6 mmol/L/h, derived). Net synthesis at the peak 28.3 +/- 3.7 g, about 19% of the meal's carbohydrate (relayed fraction); direct pathway share 46% at 2 to 4 h and 68% at 4 to 6 h.
Net liver glycogen synthesis at the peak after a liquid mixed meal
+/- 3.7 as printed. Liver only: muscle glycogen was not measured.
Liver glycogen concentration 4 h after a meal
Healthy controls (n not on the abstract), 13C NMR

+/- 60 as printed; 131 +/- 20 in type II diabetes. The search snippet attached 'fasting 23 h' and net glycogenolysis 2.8 +/- 0.7 umol/kg/min (controls) to this abstract; which interval the rate refers to was not confirmed.
Share of glucose production from gluconeogenesis, 0 to 22 h of a 68 h fast
Healthy volunteers, 13C NMR of liver glycogen plus tritiated glucose
+/- 5 as printed. The remainder (36%, derived) is net hepatic glycogenolysis.
Share of glucose production from gluconeogenesis, next 14 h
Share of glucose production from gluconeogenesis, next 18 h
+/- 1 as printed. Glycogenolysis share 4% (derived). Liver glycogen concentration at the start of the fast is not on the abstract (Nilsson and Hultman 1973 has no abstract on Europe PMC).
Liver glycogen in a 70 kg man
Standard 70 kg man, Cahill and Owen fuel-reserve table
Relayed from a search-result summary; the PDF is a scan I could not read. Depleted by about 24 h per a clinical reference in the same results (not opened).
Muscle glycogen in a 70 kg man
Same; 120 g in the Cahill and Owen table (relayed), 400 g in a Swiss review table citing Cahill (relayed)
The two versions differ by a factor of 3; the library row's '400 g in muscle and liver' matches neither exactly. No central value taken.
Adipose fat (and muscle protein) reserve in a 70 kg man
Muscle protein about 6 kg (24,000 kcal). The Swiss table gives fat 12 kg. For a 70 kg reference, not a population mean.
Muscle glycogen storage rate in the first 2 h after glycogen-depleting exercise
8 subjects after 2 h of cycling; 1.5 g/kg (5.2 +/- 0.9) or 3.0 g/kg (5.8 +/- 0.7) glucose polymer
No carbohydrate: 0.5. The difference between the doses was not significant. Second 2 h: 4.0 +/- 0.9 and 4.5 +/- 0.6.
Carbohydrate intake rate linked to the highest post-exercise glycogen synthesis
Review of short-term recovery studies; carbohydrate taken immediately after exercise
Rapid first phase 30 to 60 min, slower phase for hours; rate about 50% lower if intake is delayed by hours; absorption may limit above 1 g/min.
8 cyclists, 3 stages of 30 min at 40, 55, 75% Wmax

+/- 2 as printed; 19 +/- 2 kJ/min at 75% Wmax. Total energy expenditure and carbohydrate oxidation are not on the abstract, so a whole-body g carbohydrate per MET-hour cannot be derived from it (searched; Romijn 1993 abstract also has no rates).
Muscle glycogen used in 40 min at 75% VO2max
7 endurance-trained cyclists, three conditions (117 +/- 52 normothermic rehydrated, 172 +/- 86 and 185 +/- 97 in two hyperthermic conditions); start 434 +/- 57 mmol/kg dry muscle
A muscle concentration, not a whole-body mass: converting to grams needs the active muscle mass and dry-weight fraction, neither on the page. So no check of the built 60 g per MET-hour.
769 weight-stable adults (642 women, 127 men), 18 to 74 y, 35 to 186 kg, ventilated-hood calorimetry
+/- 0.4 as printed. The 3.5 convention overestimates by 35% on average. Body composition (fat and fat-free mass) explained 62% of variance, age 14%.
Measured resting energy expenditure per kg
+/- 0.16 as printed. The 1 kcal/kg/h convention overestimates by 20% on average. The abstract's walking subsample (49 men and 49 women, 5.6 km/h) gives no cost figure on the page.
Standard MET (activity VO2 / 3.5) minus MET relative to measured resting VO2
252 subjects, 11 activities, 2,555 measurements; mean measured MET 6.1 +/- 2.64

Abstract: standard METs were 0.51 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.59) lower (sign taken as standard minus measured). Corrected METs (activity VO2 / measured resting VO2) differed from measured by -0.02 METs (-0.11 to 0.06), not significant. 12.2% of activities misclassified by standard METs, 8.6% by METs from predicted RMR.
Doubly labeled water minus respirometry energy expenditure, low activity
5 subjects over 6 days; daily rate 1.40 +/- 0.09 x sleeping metabolic rate
Doubly labeled water minus respirometry energy expenditure, high activity
4 subjects over 3.5 days incl. 2 days of heavy bicycle ergometer work; daily rate 2.61 +/- 0.25 x sleeping metabolic rate
Non-ambulant subjects (lower limit) and elite endurance athletes (upper), from 574 DLW measurements of ages 2 to 95
Group means by age and sex are in the paper's tables, not on the abstract (searched; full text not opened).
Activity energy parameter delta for a sedentary person (cost taken proportional to body weight)
Hall Lancet model, calibrated to a sedentary PAL of 1.5 using Mifflin-St Jeor RMR
A candidate against the built scaling (cost proportional to resting rate, not body weight). TEF fixed at 10% in the same model.
Adaptive thermogenesis coefficient and time constant
fraction of intake change (time constant 14 days)
Hall Lancet model, from longitudinal weight-loss studies
tau_AT = 14 days. Not in the built path.
Change in total energy expenditure at 10% or more below usual weight
23 never-obese subjects (8 +/- 5 in 18 obese subjects); 10 to 20% weight loss by underfeeding, then maintenance
+/- 3 as printed. Resting and nonresting each fell 3 to 4 kcal/kg/d. At 10% above usual weight: +9 +/- 7 and +8 +/- 4 kcal/kg/d.
Sensitivity of fuel-use estimates to the nonprotein respiratory quotient relative to the heat equivalent of O2

Estimates 'best within 5% of the true values' when the fuel mix is assessed accurately. The abstract gives no kJ per litre O2 by fuel (searched), so the built fixed 20.1 kJ/L is not checked against it here.
Forbes parameter C in the p-ratio p = C/(C + F)
kg (times rho_L/rho_F = 0.192 in the Hall model, giving 2.0 kg, derived)
Adults; Hall Lancet appendix, Chow and Hall (p = 2/(2+F), F in kg)

Forbes cross-sectional forms: FFM = 10.4 ln(FM) + 14.2 (women) and 13.8 ln(FM) + 16.9 (men), the page says not valid at low fat mass; the 10.4 recurs in the Hall model. Hall 2007 found Forbes underestimates FFM loss for very large losses (bariatric surgery; relayed from a search summary).
Carbohydrate intake multiple needed to raise glycogen by a factor of about 1.8 (quadratic glycogen term)
Calibration statement in the Hall Lancet appendix, 'based on carbohydrate overfeeding studies with indirect calorimetry' (refs 5 and 6, not named on the text read)
The glycogen equation is an image and did not survive text extraction; the parameters are described as k_G = CI_b/G_init^2. The studies behind the calibration were not identified.
Time resolution the Hall 2006 energy-metabolism model claims
Hall 2006 AJP Endo model fitted to the Minnesota experiment

Null. A search summary stated the model 'does not attempt to simulate fluctuations of metabolism that occur within the course of a single day'; the abstract read has no such statement and the full text (PMC2377067) returned HTTP 500 through Europe PMC, and the PMC pages of the sibling papers (PMC2376744, PMC2838532) returned a browser check.
